q: A null vector is a vector that has:
o: Unit magnitude and a fixed direction
Zero magnitude and no definite direction
Zero magnitude and a direction always along the x-axis
A magnitude equal to that of its components
x: A null (zero) vector has zero magnitude and an arbitrary, undefined direction; for example P − P is a null vector. Unit magnitude describes a unit vector, the usual mix-up.

q: The unit vector in the direction of the vector 3î + 4ĵ is:
x: Magnitude = √(3² + 4²) = 5, so the unit vector is (3î + 4ĵ)/5 = 0.6î + 0.8ĵ; check: 0.36 + 0.64 = 1. Dividing by 3 + 4 = 7 instead of the magnitude is the common slip.

q: Point P has coordinates (1, 2) m and point Q has coordinates (4, 6) m. The magnitude of the displacement from P to Q is:
x: PQ = (4 − 1)î + (6 − 2)ĵ = 3î + 4ĵ, so |PQ| = √(9 + 16) = 5 m. Adding the position vectors gives (5, 8) and √89 m; the size of Q's position vector alone is √52 m.

q: Two forces, each of magnitude F, act at a point with an angle of 120° between them. The magnitude of their resultant is:
x: Take one force along x: components (F, 0) and (F cos 120°, F sin 120°) = (−F/2, √3F/2). Sum = (F/2, √3F/2), magnitude √(F²/4 + 3F²/4) = F. 2F would need the forces to be parallel; √3 F is the result for 60°.

q: The greatest and least possible resultants of two forces are 14 N and 2 N. When the two forces act at right angles to each other, their resultant is:
x: P + Q = 14 and P − Q = 2 give P = 8 N and Q = 6 N; at 90° the resultant is √(64 + 36) = 10 N. Combining 14 N and 2 N at right angles gives √200 = 10√2 N, the tempting wrong route.

q: For two vectors P and Q, the vector equation P + Q = P − Q holds. This means that:
x: Subtracting P from both sides gives Q = −Q, so 2Q = 0 and Q is the null vector. Perpendicular vectors only make the magnitudes |P + Q| and |P − Q| equal, not the vectors themselves.

q: The vector product of two parallel vectors is:
o: A scalar equal to the product of their magnitudes
x: |P × Q| = PQ sin θ, and for parallel vectors θ = 0°, so sin θ = 0 and the product is the null vector. The maximum occurs at 90°; PQ is the scalar product for parallel vectors.

q: Using the right-handed unit vectors î, ĵ and k̂, the vector product k̂ × ĵ is equal to:
x: In cyclic order ĵ × k̂ = î, and reversing the order of a vector product reverses its sign, so k̂ × ĵ = −î. Forgetting the sign change gives î.

q: For two non-zero vectors P and Q, the scalar product P · Q is equal to the magnitude of their vector product, |P × Q|. The angle between P and Q is:
x: PQ cos θ = PQ sin θ gives tan θ = 1, so θ = 45°. At 90° the scalar product is zero, and at 0° the vector product is zero, so neither can be equal.

q: Vector P = 2î + mĵ is perpendicular to vector Q = 3î − 6ĵ. The value of m is:
x: Perpendicular vectors have P · Q = 0: (2)(3) + (m)(−6) = 6 − 6m = 0, so m = 1. Dropping the minus sign of −6ĵ gives m = −1.

q: Vector P = î + 2ĵ and vector Q = 3î + k̂. The vector product P × Q is:
x: P × Q = î(2·1 − 0·0) − ĵ(1·1 − 0·3) + k̂(1·0 − 2·3) = 2î − ĵ − 6k̂. Check: its dot product with P is 2 − 2 + 0 = 0 and with Q is 6 + 0 − 6 = 0. −2î + ĵ + 6k̂ is Q × P, the reversed order.

q: A force F = (4î + 3ĵ) N acts on a body moving with velocity v = (2î − ĵ) m s⁻¹. The power delivered by the force, P = F · v, is:
x: F · v = (4)(2) + (3)(−1) = 8 − 3 = 5 W. Ignoring the minus sign gives 11 W; multiplying the magnitudes 5 × √5 assumes the vectors are parallel.

q: Torque plays the same role in rotational motion as which quantity does in linear motion?
x: A net force produces linear acceleration; a net torque produces angular acceleration, so torque is the rotational analogue of force. Mass corresponds to moment of inertia, momentum to angular momentum.

q: A force F acts along the positive y-axis at a point whose position vector from the origin lies along the positive x-axis. The direction of the torque τ = r × F about the origin is:
x: τ = r × F has the direction of î × ĵ = k̂, the positive z-axis, by the right-hand rule. Taking F × r instead gives −z; the torque is perpendicular to both r and F, never along either.

q: A force of 50 N acts at a point 0.5 m from a pivot. The force makes 30° with the line joining the pivot to that point (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = √3/2). The moment arm of the force about the pivot is:
x: Moment arm = perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action = r sin θ = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 m. Using cos 30° gives 0.25√3 m; taking the whole 0.5 m ignores the angle.

q: A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces of 10 N each, whose lines of action are 0.3 m apart. The torque of the couple is:
x: Torque of a couple = one force × perpendicular distance between the lines of action = 10 × 0.3 = 3 N m. Zero is tempting because the net force is zero, but the torques add. 6 N m counts both forces at the full 0.3 m.

q: A uniform rod 2 m long and of weight 40 N is pivoted at its lower end and held at 30° above the horizontal (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = √3/2). The torque of its weight about the pivot is:
x: The weight acts at the centre, 1 m from the pivot along the rod; its moment arm is the horizontal distance 1 × cos 30° = √3/2 m, so τ = 40 × √3/2 = 20√3 N m. Using sin 30° gives 20 N m; using the full 2 m gives 40√3 N m.

q: A wheel of radius 0.3 m on a fixed axle has a tangential force of 20 N at its rim turning it clockwise and a tangential force of 30 N on its hub, 0.1 m from the axle, turning it anticlockwise. The net torque on the wheel is:
x: Clockwise torque = 20 × 0.3 = 6 N m; anticlockwise torque = 30 × 0.1 = 3 N m; net = 3 N m clockwise. Thinking the bigger force wins gives anticlockwise; adding the torques gives 9 N m.

q: The second condition of equilibrium requires that:
o: The sum of all the forces is zero
The sum of the torques about any axis is zero
The body moves with uniform velocity
x: The second condition is Στ = 0, so there is no angular acceleration. ΣF = 0 is the first condition; a body may satisfy both and still move uniformly, so rest is not required.

q: A body is in equilibrium under the action of three coplanar forces that are not parallel. Their lines of action must:
o: Make equal angles of 120° with one another
x: If two of the lines of action meet at a point, the third force must also pass through that point, or it would have a torque about it and the second condition would fail. Equal 120° angles apply only when the three forces are equal.

q: A uniform metre rule of weight 2 N is pivoted at its 30 cm mark. A weight hung at the 10 cm mark keeps it horizontal. This weight is:
x: The rule's weight acts at 50 cm, 0.2 m from the pivot: 2 × 0.2 = 0.4 N m. The hung weight is also 0.2 m from the pivot, so W × 0.2 = 0.4 and W = 2 N. Measuring its arm from the 0 cm end instead of the pivot gives the wrong values.

q: A block of weight 60 N rests on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. It is held at rest by a horizontal force F (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = √3/2). The normal reaction of the plane on the block is:
x: Along the plane: F cos 30° = 60 sin 30°, so F = 60/√3 = 20√3 N. Perpendicular: N = 60 cos 30° + F sin 30° = 30√3 + 10√3 = 40√3 N (check: N = W/cos 30° = 120/√3 = 40√3 N). 30√3 N forgets the push of F into the plane; 20√3 N is F itself.

q: A picture hangs at rest from a nail by a string whose two halves make equal angles with the vertical. If a shorter string is used, so that the angle between the two halves increases, the tension in the string:
x: Vertically, 2T cos(θ/2) = W, where θ is the angle between the halves. As θ increases cos(θ/2) falls, so T = W/[2 cos(θ/2)] increases. Thinking a shorter string carries less load gives the wrong answer.

q: A 100 N weight hangs at rest from two strings. One string makes 60° with the horizontal and the other 30° with the horizontal, on opposite sides (sin 30° = 0.5, sin 60° = √3/2). The tension in the string at 60° to the horizontal is:
x: Horizontally T₁ cos 60° = T₂ cos 30°, so T₂ = T₁/√3; vertically T₁ sin 60° + T₂ sin 30° = 100, giving T₁(√3/2 + 1/(2√3)) = 100, so T₁ = 50√3 N and T₂ = 50 N. The strings are perpendicular, so T₁ = 100 sin 60° confirms it. 50 N is the tension in the other string.
